facts.claim: The Corps of Discovery set out up the Missouri River
facts.context: The expedition left the St Louis area in May 1804 with about 45 men.
facts.goDeeper: Jefferson's instructions were to find a practical water route across the continent. There isn't one.

facts.claim: Lewis and Clark reached the Pacific Ocean
facts.context: They sighted the Pacific in November 1805, about eighteen months out.
facts.goDeeper: Clark wrote 'Ocian in view! O! the joy' — and misspelled it.

facts.claim: The expedition returned to St Louis
facts.context: They arrived back in September 1806, having been given up for dead by many.
facts.goDeeper: Jefferson had heard nothing from them for over a year.

facts.claim: The Louisiana Purchase gave the United States the land the expedition would cross
facts.context: Bought from France in 1803, roughly doubling the size of the country.
facts.goDeeper: Jefferson had already asked Congress to fund the expedition before the purchase was agreed.

facts.claim: Distance covered by the expedition, out and back
facts.context: Roughly 8,000 miles by river, portage, horseback and on foot.
facts.goDeeper: They mapped it as they went, and Clark's maps stayed the best available for decades.

facts.claim: Amount Jefferson requested from Congress to fund the expedition
facts.context: He asked for $2,500 in a confidential message in 1803.
facts.goDeeper: The final cost came to roughly $40,000, about sixteen times the estimate.

facts.claim: Animal species new to science described by the expedition
facts.context: About 122 animals and 178 plants previously unknown to American science were recorded.
facts.goDeeper: Among them the grizzly bear, the prairie dog and the pronghorn.

facts.claim: Plant species new to science described by the expedition
facts.context: Roughly 178 plants unknown to eastern botanists were collected and described.
facts.goDeeper: Many pressed specimens survive at the Academy of Natural Sciences in Philadelphia.

facts.claim: Sergeant Charles Floyd became the expedition's only fatality
facts.context: He died in August 1804, probably of a burst appendix, which nothing then known could have treated.
facts.goDeeper: He was the only member lost, on a journey of more than two years through unmapped country.

facts.claim: Sacagawea joined the expedition at the Mandan villages
facts.context: She travelled with the Corps from spring 1805, having given birth that February.
facts.goDeeper: Her brother turned out to be a Shoshone chief, which is how the expedition got the horses it needed to cross the Rockies.

facts.claim: Sacagawea's approximate age during the expedition
facts.context: She was around 16 or 17, and carried her infant son the entire way.
facts.goDeeper: She appears on the US dollar coin issued from 2000, with her son on her back.

facts.claim: The Corps built Fort Clatsop for the winter on the Oregon coast
facts.context: Built in December 1805 near the mouth of the Columbia, where they waited out the winter.
facts.goDeeper: It rained on all but twelve of the 106 days they spent there.

facts.claim: Meriwether Lewis's age when the expedition set out
facts.context: He was 29; Clark was 33. Lewis had been Jefferson's private secretary.
facts.goDeeper: Lewis died in 1809, aged 35, of gunshot wounds on the Natchez Trace. Suicide or murder is still argued.

facts.claim: Thomas Jefferson became president
facts.context: He took office in March 1801 and began planning a western expedition almost at once.
facts.goDeeper: He had tried to organise similar expeditions three times before, and all three failed to leave.

facts.claim: The expedition found the water route across the continent it was sent to find
facts.context: There is no such route. The Rockies had to be crossed on horseback and on foot, and the crossing nearly killed them.
facts.goDeeper: Finding out that the Northwest Passage did not exist was itself the single most valuable result.

facts.claim: An enslaved man travelled with the expedition for its whole journey
facts.context: York, enslaved by Clark since childhood, made the entire journey and took a full part in it.
facts.goDeeper: He voted, on equal terms, on where to make winter camp in 1805. Clark refused him freedom for years afterwards.

facts.claim: Lewis and Clark were the first Europeans to cross North America by land
facts.context: Alexander Mackenzie crossed what is now Canada to the Pacific in 1793, twelve years earlier.
facts.goDeeper: Lewis carried a copy of Mackenzie's published account with him.

facts.claim: The whole party voted on where to spend the winter of 1805
facts.context: Every member voted, including York, an enslaved man, and Sacagawea, a Native woman.
facts.goDeeper: Neither would have been allowed to vote anywhere in the United States at the time.

facts.claim: A dog completed the entire expedition with the Corps
facts.context: Seaman, Lewis's Newfoundland, went the whole way and appears repeatedly in the journals.
facts.goDeeper: Lewis bought him for $20, a considerable sum, before setting out.

facts.claim: The expedition's journals were published promptly on its return
facts.context: Lewis was meant to prepare them and never did. A narrative appeared in 1814, and the full journals only from 1904.
facts.goDeeper: For most of the 19th century the expedition's scientific findings were effectively lost.

source.title: Journals of the Lewis and Clark Expedition
